record.paper_title: A note on the convergence of RED algorithms under minimal hypotheses and open questions
record.original_question: Consider the inverse problem y = A x̂ + e, where x̂ belongs to a low-dimensional model set Σ, A is a linear measurement map, and e is noise. Let P_Σ be a generalized projection onto Σ with the restricted β-Lipschitz property: for every z, every x in Σ, and every u in P_Σ(z), ||u − x||₂ ≤ β ||z − x||₂. The modified RED iteration is z_n = (1 − λ)x_n + λP_Σ(x_n), followed by x_{n+1} = z_n − μAᵀ(Az_n − y). A convergence bound is known when Σ is proximinal and P_Σ is close to the orthogonal projection P_Σ^⊥, specifically ||P_Σ − P_Σ^⊥||₂ ≤ η. Can one prove convergence of this modified RED iteration to a stable solution when P_Σ is only a generic restricted-Lipschitz projection, without assuming orthogonality or approximate orthogonality of the projection, as in the generalized projected-gradient-descent setting?

evidence.quote: In this note we show convergence of a slightly modified version of the RED algorithm under similar (stronger) hypotheses, and we ask open questions arising from these results.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $A:\mathbb{R}^N\to\mathbb{R}^M$ be a linear measurement operator and consider the inverse problem
$$y = A\hat x + e, \qquad \hat x \in \Sigma \subset \mathbb{R}^N,$$
where $\Sigma$ is a (low-dimensional) proximinal model set and $e\in\mathbb{R}^M$ is noise.

Generalized projection. A (possibly set-valued) map $P_\Sigma:\mathbb{R}^N\rightrightarrows \Sigma$ is called a generalized projection onto $\Sigma$. It is said to have the restricted $\beta$-Lipschitz property with respect to $\Sigma$ if
$$\forall z\in\mathbb{R}^N,\ \forall x\in\Sigma,\ \forall u\in P_\Sigma(z): \quad \|u-x\|_2 \le \beta \,\|z-x\|_2.$$
Let $P_\Sigma^{\perp}$ denote an orthogonal projection onto $\Sigma$ (a selection minimizing $\|z-\cdot\|_2$ over $\Sigma$).

Modified RED iteration. For step sizes $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\mu>0$, and an initial point $x_0\in\mathbb{R}^N$, define
$$z_n = (1-\lambda)x_n + \lambda P_\Sigma(x_n), \qquad x_{n+1} = z_n - \mu A^\top(Az_n - y).$$

Known result. Let $\beta = \beta_\Sigma(P_\Sigma)$ be the restricted Lipschitz constant and let $\delta=\delta_\Sigma(\mu A^\top A)$ be a restricted contraction constant of $I-\mu A^\top A$ on $\Sigma$. Assume $\|P_\Sigma - P_\Sigma^{\perp}\|_2 \le \eta$ in the sense that any selection of $P_\Sigma$ stays within distance $\eta$ of $P_\Sigma^{\perp}$. If
$$r := \delta\beta + |1-\lambda|\,\|I-\mu A^\top A\|_{op} < 1,$$
then
$$\|x_n-\hat x\|_2 \le r^n \|x_0-\hat x\|_2 + \frac{1}{1-r}\bigl(|1-\lambda|\,\|I-\mu A^\top A\|_{op}\,\eta + \mu\,\|A^\top e\|_2\bigr).$$

Question. Drop the closeness-to-orthogonality assumption $\|P_\Sigma - P_\Sigma^\perp\|_2 \le \eta$. Does the modified RED iteration above still converge to a stable solution of the inverse problem under only the assumption that $P_\Sigma$ is a generic restricted-$\beta$-Lipschitz generalized projection onto the proximinal set $\Sigma$ (i.e., in the same generality as the generalized projected-gradient-descent setting), and if so, under what conditions on $\lambda,\mu,\beta,A,\Sigma$ can one obtain a quantitative error bound analogous to the one above but without the $\eta$ term?
artifact.status_search_result: The question is explicitly posed as an open problem about extending the convergence analysis of the modified RED iteration to generic restricted-Lipschitz generalized projections, parallel to known results for generalized projected gradient descent. Web searches did not surface a published resolution of this specific question.

status_evidence.title: On Asymptotic Linear Convergence of Projected Gradient Methods
status_evidence.snippet: Local linear convergence analysis for projected gradient methods requiring Lipschitz-continuous differentiability of the projection operator.
status_evidence.claim: Related convergence theory for projected gradient methods exists but does not directly resolve the modified RED question without orthogonality assumptions.
